titre: The Myth of the Left Brain and the Right Brain
accroche: Logical on the left, creative on the right: MRI scans of 1,011 brains find no trace of this dominance.
contenu_vulgarise:
An online test promises to reveal whether you are more “left-brained,” analytical and rigorous, or “right-brained,” intuitive and creative. The test has a flaw: no brain imaging data supports the idea that an individual would preferentially use an entire hemisphere.

## What Is True, and What Is Not

Lateralization does exist, but locally, not globally. Language, for example, almost always depends on the left hemisphere: a study of 326 healthy subjects measured right-sided language dominance in only 4% of strongly right-handed people. Spatial attention, conversely, leans toward the right hemisphere. These are solid facts.

What does not follow is the leap to personality: the idea that an individual would “function” with one hemisphere overall more active, stronger, more connected than the other, logical on the left, creative on the right. In 2013, a team from the University of Utah tested this hypothesis directly with resting-state functional connectivity MRI, on 1,011 brains aged 7 to 29. Result: the lateralization of brain connections is a local property, network by network, not a global property of the individual. The data are not consistent with the idea of a “more left-brained” or “more right-brained” phenotype.

Jeff Anderson, coauthor of the study, sums it up this way: “It is entirely true that certain brain functions are housed on one side or the other of the brain. Language tends to be on the left, attention more on the right. But people don't tend to have a stronger brain network on one side than the other.”

## Where the Confusion Comes From

The myth latches onto the very real work of Roger Sperry on split-brain patients, rewarded with a Nobel Prize in 1981. Sperry showed that the two hemispheres, surgically separated, process information differently. But these observations concerned patients whose corpus callosum had been cut, not intact brains. In the 1970s, the popular press and then self-help books, including Betty Edwards's famous *Drawing on the Right Side of the Brain*, extended this surgical dissociation into a theory of personality, with no data to back it.

The intact brain does not divide into two camps. It works as a set of specialized networks, distributed on both sides, that cooperate constantly, a less clear-cut picture than a left-versus-right match, but one that corresponds to what imaging actually shows.

carte.punch: “Left brain” or “right brain”: an MRI study of 1,011 people found neither.
carte.idee: Language leans toward the left hemisphere, attention toward the right, but nothing in the MRI scans of 1,011 brains shows that an individual would preferentially use an entire hemisphere. The myth comes from an unwarranted extrapolation of the real work on split-brain patients.

quiz.question: What exactly does the 2013 study of 1,011 brains show, contrary to what the “left brain / right brain” myth suggests?
choix: That no brain function is ever lateralized to one side or the other
That lateralization exists network by network, but does not add up to a global dominance of one hemisphere
That men have a more developed left hemisphere and women a more developed right hemisphere
That the right hemisphere takes part in no language task
quiz.explication: Some functions are indeed lateralized, language more to the left, attention more to the right, but the study finds no evidence that an individual has, overall, a structurally dominant hemisphere. Lateralization is a local property of specific networks, not a global personality trait.
